claim: A causal intervention replaces a structural assignment; SWIG single-world restrictions need not impose the independent-error model's cross-world restrictions.
The constructed banking diagram distinguishes assignment, receipt, outcome and inclusion; d-separation and latent graph classes determine admissible operations.
Truncated factorization, back-door and front-door derivations give distinct observable functionals under specified support and structural restrictions.
ID/IDC operate on intervention kernels in their graph class; a hedge certifies nonidentification, while unsupported software alone does not.
Two strictly positive binary observed laws coincide while ATEs differ; consistency bounds and a collider-selected contrast can be checked by finite enumeration.
Linear IV follows from structural exclusion, conditional moments and relevance; 2SLS/GMM are moment estimators whose variance depends on the score sampling law.
The binary Wald ratio equals LATE under monotonicity and the other stated IV conditions; two compliant completions leave the observed law fixed but change the population ATE.

A local-to-zero first stage yields a nondegenerate ratio limit; Gaussian fixed-design AR inversion has an exact F law without first-stage rank strength. A known-covariance Gaussian ratio experiment can return disconnected or unbounded sets. Heteroskedastic, clustered and learned-instrument uniform inference requires further conditions.
The partially linear IV score is nuisance-orthogonal but still requires relevance; a nonlinear IV response solves an operator inverse problem whose injectivity cannot be created by prediction.
The ATE functional has the displayed canonical gradient in the unrestricted independent observed-data model; AIPW has an exact product remainder and conditional double robustness.

Response, X, R, DR and generalized forest methods target effects through different fitted objects; a constant R-loss projection is overlap weighted, and CATE rates require more than the ATE error condition.
A balanced coarsening of a sufficient covariate can retain exchangeability; arbitrary lossy representations can discard confounding information.
Sequential mechanism replacement, g-computation, backward evaluation and IP weighting agree under the specified longitudinal information and support assumptions.
MSMs parameterize regime means and SNMMs conditional blips; g-estimation enforces treatment-residual mean moments, not individual counterfactual reconstruction.
Recursive augmentation admits the displayed true-score and two-period bias identities; richer sequential robustness and propensity-dependent policies need their corresponding constructions.
A common controlled generative law yields both the observational likelihood and model-conditional policy replacement; observed-history logging permits reduction to longitudinal history kernels.

Private action selection changes the filtered posterior; intervention removes that action-likelihood update. Forward recursion agrees with latent-path enumeration, and smoothing cannot be a prospective feature.
Belief-state planning assumes a supplied invariant environment; observational HMM identification, causal law identification and policy-value identification are different questions.

Proposed result types and adapters must preserve target, identification state, support, moment/likelihood, dependence and approximation; these are design consequences, not implemented general software.
An inverse problem can identify a linear functional without identifying its whole response; null-space orthogonality and adjoint range distinguish identification and stability.

Known-operator sequence risk exposes the bias-variance tradeoff; Hall-Horowitz Theorem 4.1 gives a distinct estimated-operator rate under A.1--A.5, whose normal-operator eigenvalues cannot be confused with conditional-operator singular values.

Proxy exclusions, bridge existence and latent completeness imply the proximal mean; bridge uniqueness and causal-average uniqueness are distinct. The binary example recovers effect 2 from a raw contrast 3.8.

The two-bridge augmented expression has an exact mixed-product remainder; inference depends on projected errors and ill-posedness. A minimax conditional-moment loss differs from factual outcome regression.
Differentiating successive observation kernels yields the finite-horizon longitudinal canonical gradient and orthogonal variance decomposition for fixed policies and independent trajectories.

The general longitudinal bias telescopes into time-specific nuisance products; conditional unbiased pseudo-outcome recursion explains sequential robustness and why arbitrary regression specifications are insufficient.

Backward bounded logistic fluctuations solve the longitudinal residual score equations, subject to finite optimizers and correct rule evaluation; score solving and nuisance-rate/empirical-process conditions are separate.

A single-period targeting update solves the empirical ATE score but updated fits still need product-rate and empirical-process control; fitting the fluctuation on held-out data introduces dependence on that data.
Strict exogeneity justifies static within moments, while RE covariance and correlated-effects mean restrictions use additional between-unit information.
Differencing creates lagged-outcome endogeneity; valid earlier lag moments depend on the assignment/error clock, and second-order residual correlation probes a key restriction.
Conditional untreated parallel trends identify ATT through regression, weighting and a doubly robust functional whose displayed bias is a nuisance product.
Staggered and reversible treatment designs target different path contrasts; cohort composition and possibly negative TWFE weights change the estimand.
Synthetic-control loading balance removes factor bias, but pretreatment fit requires rank and approximation conditions and does not establish placebo exchangeability.
Score covariance determines panel information; multiway DML requires exchangeability, dissociation and growing cluster dimensions rather than arbitrary serial dependence.
Gaussian structural shocks are rotationally ambiguous; non-Gaussian SVAR identification adds independent innovations and acyclic instantaneous restrictions.
External-instrument dynamic response ratios require off-date as well as contemporaneous exclusions, normalization and relevant instrument variation; LP and VAR recovery impose distinct conditions.
Subsampling, aggregation and state-coordinate changes have different effects on intervention identification; distinct fine-scale or structural laws can agree observationally.
Time-series inference concerns the score process and horizon dependence; Granger dependence concerns a specified predictive information set, with additional restrictions required for causality.

ADMG latent projections and MAG/PAG discovery objects preserve different causal information; invariant endpoint marks and m-separation do not justify treating every directed mixed-graph edge as unconfounded.
PC oracle recovery uses faithfulness and separating sets; high-dimensional finite-sample consistency requires the cited Gaussian, sparsity and signal-strength assumptions.
Trace-exponential acyclicity follows from nonnegative closed-walk terms, while functional-model direction identification requires additional noise and function restrictions.
PCMCI+ and LPCMCI target different graph classes under their own sufficiency, observation, lag and stationarity restrictions; enlarging a latent time window can change old adjacencies.
Generalized adjustment is sound and complete for adjustment under amenability, forbidden-set exclusion and blocking conditions in the stated no-selection graph classes.
Graph uncertainty induces a union of causal effect sets; the Gaussian three-node chain class has effects {0,1/4} despite an identical observed law.
Observation kernels and availability/version clocks constrain identification and prospective measurability; a deterministic cleaning operation cannot distinguish already equivalent observed laws.

MAR outcome means have an augmented nuisance-product identity; without missingness restrictions the same binary recorded law permits means 1/4 and 3/4, while missing-data discovery needs its own assumptions.

Known nondifferential misclassification is an invertible matrix problem; unknown or singular error mechanisms cannot be repaired by generic cleaning, and high-dimensional denoising requires structure.

Entity linkage uncertainty contributes between-linkage variance and can change intervention units; injective transformations preserve information while coarsening and changed outcome scales can alter targets.
Known full-rank emissions, independent randomized supported actions and positive state mass identify finite controlled transitions and reward means through the displayed left-inverse equations.

Controlled EM and particle likelihoods must retain private action-selection factors; Gaussian filters, latent-parameter posteriors and numerical approximations solve distinct statistical problems.
Fixed-policy reward/transition and Bellman-residual bounds quantify model/numerical error under a common controlled state system, without resolving causal ambiguity.

Dynamic logit choice inversion leaves a state-dependent reference-payoff vector unidentified; potential shifts preserve historical choices but need not preserve a counterfactual with changed transitions.
Nested-solve, CCP and joint Bayesian-DP estimation use different computation and regularity; likelihood tolerance is distinct from preference identification or posterior accuracy.
Recursive ID extracts a fixed-mediator district kernel in the front-door trace; IDC can identify a conditional intervention when its joint distribution is not identified.
Edge-specific natural mediation invokes a stronger structural model; a fresh randomized mediator intervention has a different g-functional and need not decompose the original total effect.
Incremental odds policies preserve support but depend on the behavior law; their gradient includes the treatment-score derivative and reduces to Y minus its mean at delta one.
Natural-action and stochastic LMTPs need different randomization assumptions; transformed densities sum inverse branches, and the fixed-map gradient includes variation in the natural action law.

Censoring enters the longitudinal factorization at its own observation clock and requires joint treatment/retention exchangeability and support; the displayed weights follow by sequential cancellation.
Competing-event category probabilities and ordered hazards use different within-period denominators; lowering the default hazard can raise cumulative default incidence by retaining more exposure.

Policy-specific eligibility changes the population and produces a ratio gradient; the source eligible-treatment effect holds the prior path fixed and does not identify an always-eligible cross-world stratum.

Policy regret separates uniform score estimation, nuisance-product bias and optimization error; the primary VC theorem needs stronger uniform/nuisance/noise restrictions than an ATE central limit theorem.

Known predictable randomization yields a mean-zero contrast martingale; a Gaussian mixture gives the stated simultaneous-in-time boundary, without generic validity for observational fits or delayed outcome selection.

A partial-interference exposure map and known exposure probabilities identify a finite-population exposure mean; cluster-only randomization cannot separate unsupported individual and spillover effects.
Selection diagrams encode mechanism differences; S-admissibility supports covariate transport, while a changed proxy kernel can invalidate the same reweighting operation.

Invariant prediction's intersection argument controls false inclusions when a true invariant subset is tested validly; it does not guarantee recovery of all parents or validity after arbitrary screening.
A scalar monotone triangular first stage recovers a conditional rank, but average response needs joint rank/action support; conditional and transported compliance weights define distinct targets.
Local CATE rates require smoother stability and weighted local nuisance-product errors; oracle equivalence does not eliminate smoothing bias or provide simultaneous coverage.

Changing assignment marks, decision clocks and deterministic event regimes are distinct operations; regime adherence identification uses consistency and compensator exchangeability.

State-dependent silent observation intervals affect filtering, and an externally scheduled observation intervention must replace that information mechanism.

Adversarial treatment-group balance alone does not establish preservation of confounding information in a representation.

SCM-prior amortization cannot distinguish observationally equivalent causal explanations; generic influence-function correction is not a longitudinal coverage theorem.
ProximalFM's oracle consistency requires identification under its prior, while proxy width/cardinality heuristics and finite-K neural training do not prove it.
